'''Ichinomiya Gozen Shrine''' (一之御前神社) is a shrine located in Aichi Prefecture, Nagoya, Atsuta Ward. It is one of the Keidai-Sessha of Atsuta Shrine.

==Overview==
The founding is said to have occurred either during the era of Keikō Emperor or during the reign of Tenmu Emperor {{#tag:ref|"'The palace of the Sun (Emperor Keikō) and the establishment of a separately enshrined Aramitama deity' (from "Atsuta Shrine Historical Records: Compilation of Origins": page 139)"|group="Note"}}. It is located to the northwest of the main shrine, at the far end of the pilgrimage path known as "Kokoro no Komichi", and was relocated to its present site in 1893 (Meiji 26); prior to that, it stood near the southeast of the current main shrine {{#tag:ref|"From the perspective of the former main hall, the direction was still to the northwest. (From "April 1893 Atsuta Shrine Reconstruction and Pre-Meiji Structures Location Estimation Diagram": <ref name="名古屋市史地図">"Nagoya City History Map"</ref>)"|group="Note"}}.

It enshrines '''Amaterasu Omikami Aramitama''' (あまてらすおおかみあらみたま) as its deity<ref name="神宮20"/>. The term "Aramitama" refers to a divine spirit that generates fierce, dynamic phenomena and is seen as a symbol of valor and initiative. The reason for its enshrinement at Atsuta Shrine is understood to be equivalent to the existence of Ise Grand Shrine's Aramatsuri-no-Miya <small>({{Coord|34|27|22|N|136|43|30|E|scale:2500}})</small><ref name="神宮20"/>.

Referred to as "'The First Attendant Deity of the Imperial Court'" {{#tag:ref|"From 'Atsuta Shrine Official Enshrinement Record' <ref name="神宮史料縁起由緒139"/> and 'Atsuta Shrine Record' <ref name="神宮史料縁起由緒363">"Atsuta Shrine Historical Records: Compilation of Origins": page 363</ref>, etc."|group="Note"}}, the shrine not only shares an extremely close relationship with the main shrine but also gives the impression of a loyal, trusted aide. During the main shrine's rituals, it was long customary to first present offerings here—a practice said to carry the meaning of "oni-gui" (poison tasting) {{#tag:ref|"'When enshrining the main shrine, offerings are first prepared at Aramisaki, as is commonly said to be 'oni-gui'' (from "Oshu Shrine Secret Tradition": <ref name="神宮史料縁起由緒続一7">"Atsuta Shrine Historical Records: Continued Compilation of Origins (Part I)": page 7</ref>)"|group="Note"}}.
<br/>From this, an alternative theory has long existed proposing that, either as a different deity or as a supplementary spirit, Ootomo Takehito no Mikoto was enshrined. While Amano Nobukage and Fukada Masakazu support this theory, Tsuda Masao dismisses it as "inconceivable"<ref name="地名考75">"Owari Province Place Name Studies": page 75</ref>. According to the "Owari Chronicle", Ootomo Takehito no Mikoto was a warrior who, during Yamato Takeru's eastern expedition, served as a deputy general on both flanks alongside Kibi no Takehiko (きびたけひこのみこと) {{#tag:ref|"From the Nihon Shoki (Volume 7, Emperor Keikō)"<ref name="日本書紀上289">"Kazana Nihon Shoki, Volume 1": page 289</ref>|group="Note"}}, and it is said that the placement of this shrine and Ryujinja (whose enshrined deity is Kibi Takehiko no Mikoto) flanking the main shrine like guards originates from this account<ref name="尾張志熱田9">"Owari Chronicle Atsuta": page 9</ref>.
<br/>Before the Edo period, it appears that Ryujinja and this shrine were regarded as a combined entity, and a petition requesting that they be recognized as separate shrines was submitted to the chief priest (dated June 5, 1686 (Jōkyō 3 April 15))<ref name="神宮史料造営遷宮上412">"Atsuta Shrine Historical Records: Construction and Relocation, Volume I": page 412</ref>{{#tag:ref|"Request stating 'Separate shrines for Ichinomiya and Ryujinja'."|group="Note"}}. This request was granted, and since then, Ichinomiya Gozen Shrine and Ryujinja have existed independently.

As for the origin of the shrine's name, works such as Wahimeimyojoseki note that the character "魂" can be read as "Misaki", giving rise to the theory that it was written as "Ichinomisaki" (一ノ魂) {{#tag:ref|"From 'Atsuta Main and Subsidiary Shrine Divine Body Sacred Decree Collection Theory'"<ref name="神宮史料縁起由緒続一34">"Atsuta Shrine Historical Records: Continued Compilation of Origins (Part I)": page 34</ref>|group="Note"}}. Another theory holds that the temporary shrine—where the Grass-cutting Sword (also known as the Kusanagi Sword), which was returned to the court in 686 (the first year of Shuchō), was first enshrined—gave the shrine its name<ref name="神宮史料縁起由緒続一184">"Atsuta Shrine Historical Records: Continued Compilation of Origins (Part I)": page 184</ref>. Furthermore, according to the "Owari Chronicle", since the main shrine enshrines five deities—Amaterasu Ōmikami, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Prince Yamato Takeru, Miyasu-hime and Takeinadane no Mikoto—there is a theory that the name specifically refers to Amaterasu Omikami herself, the foremost of these deities {{#tag:ref|"From 'Owari Chronicle Atsuta': <ref name="尾張志熱田8">page 8</ref> and 'Atsuta Shrine Record': <ref name="神宮史料縁起由緒363"/>"group="Note"}}. It has also been written as "Ichinokami-mae" (一神前) {{#tag:ref|"From 'Atsuta Shrine Official Enshrinement Record'"<ref name="神宮史料縁起由緒139"/>|group="Note"}}, and as "Ichimusaki" (一御崎) {{#tag:ref|"From 'Atsuta Main and Subsidiary Shrine Divine Body Sacred Decree Collection'"<ref name="神宮史料縁起由緒171">page 171</ref>|group="Note"}}.
